extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of probability, statistics, and philosophy of scientific induction (advanced undergraduates, graduate students, researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles for inductive inference using the 'inverse method' (Laplacean/Bayesian-style reasoning) illustrated by urn/ballot-box models and examples from astronomy and spectroscopy. Focuses on how to convert observed frequencies into probabilities for hypotheses and future events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballot-box representation of events and hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent the happening of an event by drawing a white ball and failure by a black ball from a ballot-box whose contents (ratio white:black) are unknown; hypotheses correspond to possible contents (proportions) of the box.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the canonical concrete model for the inverse problem: observations (draws with replacement) give evidence about the urn's composition; reasoning about future events is reduced to reasoning about hypotheses on the urn composition. The model supports both finite-hypothesis enumeration (few possible urn compositions) and continuous families (varying proportion of white balls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing-boxes rule (probability of origin after mixing)
rubrics_metrics.description: If several boxes (each with given numbers of white and black balls) are mixed and a white ball drawn from the aggregate, the probability that it came from a particular original box equals the number of white balls in that particular box divided by the total number of white balls in all boxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this identity to relate composite/hierarchical hypotheses to observed outcomes; demonstrated with example of three boxes each containing ten balls with differing counts of white balls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse-method (likelihood-weighted hypothesis probabilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: To infer hypotheses from data: enumerate applicable hypotheses, compute for each hypothesis the probability (likelihood) that the observed data would occur under that hypothesis, weight hypotheses proportionally to those likelihoods, then normalize so the hypothesis probabilities sum to unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematicians compute the probability of each hypothesis given the observed data by using the inverse (Bayesian) method; once hypothesis probabilities are obtained, deduce probabilities for future events by averaging (summing) over hypotheses the product of hypothesis probability and the event probability conditional on that hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-hypotheses (Condorcet) procedure: compute, proportion, normalize
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible hypotheses are finitely many and discrete (e.g., urn contains 0,1,2,3,4 white balls), compute for each hypothesis the probability of observed sequence (accounting for order multiplicity), then make their absolute probabilities proportional to those computed values and normalize (divide by sum) to obtain posterior probabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Condorcet/Lacroix example with four-ball urn and observed three whites and one black: compute likelihood for each composition, multiply by combinatorial factor for order, sum likelihoods (27+16+3 = 46), divide to normalize and then compute predictive probability for next draw by averaging over hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: General continuous-hypotheses solution (Laplace infinite-urn / uniform prior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the proportion of white balls as ranging continuously (limit of large finite urn) and sum (integrate) the contributions of infinitely many hypotheses using integral calculus; Laplace's standard assumption corresponds to a uniform prior over the proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This device yields compact, general formulas for predictive probabilities. The text notes Boole's objections to the arbitrariness of the assumption but defends it on grounds that it is less arbitrary than alternatives, closely approximates large finite-urn results, and yields simple usable formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule: probability next when event observed m times without failure
rubrics_metrics.description: If an event has been observed m times and never failed, the probability it will happen on the next occasion is (m+1)/(m+2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as Rule I. Example interpretations: with m successes in m trials (with replacement), one should not conclude certainty; the formula quantifies the degree of belief for the immediate next occurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule: probability of continuing success for n more occasions (no prior failures)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an event has happened m times and has not yet failed, the probability that it will happen n more times in succession is (m+1)/(m+1+n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as Rule 2. Use this to compute the chance that a regularly-observed phenomenon will repeat for a specified short run; the probability decreases as the extrapolation length n increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule: probability next when event happened m times and failed n times
rubrics_metrics.description: If an event has happened m times and failed n times, the probability it will happen on the next occasion is (m+1)/(m+n+2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This general formula unifies cases with prior failures and successes; examples include estimating whether the next discovered element will be metallic or whether a next examined metal will be less dense than water, using observed counts and adding a +1 'pseudocount' to each outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multinomial/multiple-outcome rule (counts +1 prior; new outcomes assigned 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: When mutually exclusive events A,B,C,... have been observed m,n,p,... times respectively and one of them must occur, their probabilities are proportional to m+1, n+1, p+1, ...; if new (previously unseen) outcomes are possible, assign prior weight 1 to each such new outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus the absolute probability of A = (m+1)/(m+1+n+1+p+1+ ... [+1 for possible new outcomes]). This is the generalization of the (m+1)/(m+n+2) device to multiple categories and includes the prior allowance for unseen categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalize likelihoods to get absolute hypothesis probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The absolute probability of each hypothesis is proportional to the probability that the observed events would follow from it; to obtain absolute probabilities divide each proportional value by the sum over all hypotheses so that total certainty (=1) is achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restates the normalization step of the inverse method and is demonstrated in the discrete Condorcet example (divide by 46) and in continuous cases by integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiplication of small independent probabilities to reject chance (coincidence inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple independent coincidences are observed, multiply the small individual probabilities of each coincidence under chance; if the resulting joint probability is astronomically small, the hypothesis of casual coincidence is extremely unlikely and a common cause is strongly supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications: matching spectral lines (Bunsen & Kirchhoff) — sixty matching lines give probability ~ (1/2)^60; Michell's astronomical cluster/double-star calculations. Caveat: account for instrumental resolution and model assumptions when estimating individual coincidence probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish odds from probabilities; odds progression with successive observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Odds after successive observations of the same casual event grow as 2:1, 3:1, 4:1, ... (i.e., after k observations the odds are (k+1):1), while the corresponding probabilities are (k+1)/(k+2), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes the difference between stating odds and probabilities and gives the pilot-fish/shark example. Use odds-language when comparing likelihood ratios; convert to probabilities when needed for predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: inference weakens when extrapolating far beyond data
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience-based inferences increase probability for near-future events but lose much of their certainty when pushed far beyond the range of observations; extreme extrapolations (e.g., asserting persistence 'for all time') are unjustified by finite experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the sun-rise example (even with vast past occurrences the probability of continued rising approaches but is not equal to certainty for arbitrarily long horizons). Quotation of De Morgan is used to underscore the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model-assumption scrutiny and robustness (Laplace prior caveat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that Laplace's assumption (uniform prior over proportions / infinite-urn model) is to some degree arbitrary; however, it is defended as comprehensive, yielding results close to those from large finite models and producing simple, usable formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text acknowledges objections (e.g., Boole) and lists three replies: (1) the uniform/infinite assumption is less arbitrary than alternatives, (2) results approximate large finite-urn models, (3) it yields simple formulas that seem reasonable to an experienced understanding. Use this as a rubric to assess sensitivity of conclusions to prior/model choices.
